channel.title: Personal News Feed — News & World Affairs
channel.description: Personally scored news, world affairs, opinion/analysis & foreign affairs, business & finance, and San Diego/local articles curated by news-filter

item.title: UK retail sales rise on emergency supply demand
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: UK retail sales jump as consumers stock up on emergency supplies
UK retail sales rose 0.7% in October as consumers stocked up on emergency supplies following the government’s ‘Be Ready Campaign.’ Food sales jumped 0.8% amid warnings about cyber attacks, extreme weather, and other emergencies. Clothing sales rebounded after a warm spell ended, while fuel sales fell due to higher petrol prices. Oliver Vernon-Harcourt of Deloitte called the growth a ‘reassuring start’ to the holiday retail season. Consumer confidence remained negative, with GfK’s index at minus 22. The Bank of England raised rates to 4%, and energy bills are set to rise 26% in January. Paul Dales of Capital Economics warned households may not sustain spending amid inflation pressures. The government borrowed £17bn in October, with overall debt at £3.1tn, or 95.8% of GDP.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Surge, Prompting Debate Over Waiting to Buy Homes
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: With Mortgage Rates Rising, Should You Hibernate Until Spring?
Mortgage rates surged 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov. 19, wiping out recent declines. A $400,000 loan would see monthly payments rise by $78. The spike follows inflation reports showing higher-than-expected consumer and wholesale price increases. Federal Reserve policymakers expect inflation to remain above their 2% target, with a potential rate hike anticipated at the Dec. 8-9 meeting. While waiting until spring could offer more home options, data shows a broader slowdown in sales, with pending home sales down 16.7% in October. NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun warned annual sales could fall to their lowest level since the mid-1990s. Buyers are advised to strengthen finances through debt reduction, credit improvement, or larger down payments. Sellers may face less competition in winter, offering room for negotiation on price, closing costs, or repairs. However, spring could bring both more homes and more buyers, potentially offsetting lower rates.

item.title: La Mesa Implements Road Safety Measures to Enhance Walkability
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: La Mesa works to improve road safety with new street designs and traffic-calming measures
La Mesa is enhancing road safety with new street designs and traffic-calming measures amid concerns over rainy weather risks. City officials are targeting high-risk intersections for improvements, including pedestrian bridges, bike lanes, sidewalks, and roundabouts to boost walkability. Councilmember Laura Lothian emphasized the importance of pedestrian access, particularly in the Village. The La Mesa Boulevard Complete Streets Plan includes recycled rubber speed humps and additional stop signs at intersections. The city installed its first roundabout at El Paso Street and Dalhart Avenue in August, aiming to slow traffic in a busy area. Lothian noted the roundabout effectively reduces speeding on fast-moving streets. While projects are costly, officials view them as part of a broader safety initiative. Ongoing efforts focus on identifying problem areas and expanding improvements to make roads safer for all users.

item.title: European Leaders Seek Direct Peace Talks with Russia Over Ukraine Conflict
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle Original headline: European Leaders Push for Inclusive Peace Talks with Russia in Ukraine Conflict
European leaders have agreed to pursue direct peace talks with Russia to end the Ukraine war, with Germany, France, the UK, Poland, and Italy leading negotiations. At the Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz confirmed talks would occur 'soon,' while UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham emphasized a 'clear and consistent' European position. French President Emmanuel Macron warned Russia's 'maximalist demands' are unrealistic. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reiterated Russia's rejection of all proposals but acknowledged potential for NATO-style security guarantees, which Moscow has expressed 'comfortability' with. Russian President Vladimir Putin, during a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, acknowledged European interest in talks but stressed Russia seeks clarity on Europe's contributions. Putin invited leaders to Moscow to outline positions, stating dialogue with Ukraine must follow. U.S. envoy Jared Kushner noted Trump remains committed to a peace deal with European involvement. The summit condemned Russia's 'systematic escalation' of attacks on Ukraine and called for an 'energy ceasefire' during winter, along with 'robust and legally binding security guarantees.' German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called the summit a 'success,' stressing support for Ukraine militarily and logistically. Merz criticized the Shenzhen trilateral talks, comparing them to the 1945 Yalta Conference, warning against similar divisions in Ukraine's case. The meeting marked renewed efforts for multilateral engagement, with European leaders insisting on shaping peace terms directly.

item.title: Japan's inflation data supports BoJ's plan for December rate hike
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: October inflation data keeps BoJ on course for further tightening
Japan's October CPI inflation rose to 2.3% annual rate, below expectations but above September's 2.1% increase. Core inflation, excluding fresh food but including energy, climbed to 2.2% from 2.1%. Energy prices surged due to the phased-out government fuel and bill subsidies, with gas prices up 5.8% annually and electricity prices rising 1.6%. Supercore inflation, excluding food and energy, was 2.2%, slightly below September's 2.4% but still above the BoJ's 2% target. The Bank of Japan remains on track to raise interest rates at its December meeting, with further tightening expected in 2027 as price pressures persist.

item.title: U.K. and EU hold summit to address post-Brexit relations
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties
The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties. Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets with EU officials to address post-Brexit relations, seeking to mend ties and explore potential rejoining. Burnham describes the summit as a step toward undoing Brexit's damage, acknowledging its economic and social costs. He advocates for closer cooperation, including agreements on youth mobility, trade, and emissions. Deals include up to 100,000 young adults from the U.K. and EU working in each other's countries, eased food trade checks, and an emissions trading agreement. Burnham claims these could boost the U.K. economy by 0.4%. EU officials, including President Ursula von der Leyen, emphasize ambition and concrete results, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage warns the Brexit debate is resurfacing. EU officials remain cautious, wary of past shifting demands and seeking clarity on the U.K.'s intentions. Ireland's ambassador highlights the need for clear decisions on Brexit's future.

item.title: Block's Structure Flattened, Three Core Roles Defined
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Jack Dorsey says Block is now a lot flatter and has 3 'significant roles' for staff
Jack Dorsey describes Block's workforce as 'a lot more flat' following recent layoffs. The company now operates with fewer hierarchical layers, emphasizing 'assignment' over 'command and control.' Dorsey explained that remote work and automation led to a restructuring, reducing reliance on communication hierarchies. Block has streamlined roles into three categories: individual contributors (ICs), directly responsible individuals (DRIs), and coaches. Coaches, previously called managers, support ICs and DRIs without traditional oversight. Dorsey noted that ICs and DRIs now have full access to company data, enabling 'context-rich decisions' without constant input. The shift aligns with broader industry trends like the 'Great Flattening,' where companies like Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta have eliminated middle layers. Dorsey highlighted that intelligence tools and smaller teams are enabling a 'new way of working' that changes how companies operate. The changes follow Block's February layoff, which cut nearly half its workforce.

item.title: Europeans Seek to Replace UN Peacekeepers in Lebanon
item.description:
Source: Washington Post - World Original headline: Seeking Mideast role, Europeans push to replace U.N. peacekeepers in Lebanon
Europeans push to replace U.N. peacekeepers in Lebanon with a European force, led by France, as the U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) prepares to withdraw by year-end. The plan faces Israeli opposition, with U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz visiting Beirut to explore alternatives. France proposes a smaller force of 2,000-5,000 troops, down from UNIFIL’s 7,500. European leaders, including Italy’s Guido Crosetto and the E.U.’s Kaja Kallas, emphasize the need for a U.N. mandate and parliamentary approval. Israel warns against foreign forces, arguing no international force can restrain Hezbollah. Lebanese officials warn a vacuum would worsen regional tensions. UNIFIL, established in 1978, has also played an economic role in southern Lebanon, funding local projects and coordinating humanitarian aid. Critics accuse UNIFIL of failing to counter Hezbollah attacks, but analysts note its role is supplementary. Hezbollah opposes private security firms replacing UNIFIL but remains silent on European plans. The U.N. Security Council must approve the transition, with France holding key leverage. Lebanon’s Health Ministry reports 4,300 deaths and 12,400 injuries from Israeli-Hezbollah clashes since March.

item.title: Southern California faces flash floods, rescues after heavy rain
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Heavy rain drenches Southern California, prompting rescues, flash flood concerns
Heavy rain from an atmospheric river hit Southern California, causing road closures, flash flood warnings, and rescues. The National Weather Service reported rainfall rates exceeding an inch per hour, triggering multiple warnings. Highway 1 in Santa Barbara County was closed, and firefighters conducted swift-water rescues in Santa Clarita. Flooding affected freeways and caused debris flows, with trees snapped in Los Angeles. Evacuation warnings were issued for fire-scarred areas like Pacific Palisades and Malibu, later lifted. A woman was rescued from Tujunga Wash, and a man and his dog were saved from floodwaters. The storm, part of a strong El Niño, led to state prepositioning of emergency resources. Northern California also faced heavy rain, with submerged vehicles in San Francisco. Officials urged caution near flood channels, noting ongoing risks for homeless individuals camping near waterways.

item.title: Uruguay builds national care system as public infrastructure
item.description:
Source: Vox Original headline: How Uruguay built a national care system from the ground up
Uruguay established a national care system by law in 2015, creating the National Integrated Care System (SNIC) to provide childcare, eldercare, and disability support as universal rights. The system covers 78,000 children in early education, 6,000 disabled individuals, and elderly care services through community-run centers and government-funded assistants. Feminist organizing, including a 2003 time-use survey showing women did 2/3 of unpaid care work, drove the policy. The law prioritizes services over cash payments, treats care as a right for all, and mandates legal protections to prevent reversal. Despite challenges like funding gaps and long waitlists, Uruguay’s model influences global debates, with advocates like Ai-jen Poo calling it a social insurance model akin to Social Security. Holly Milburn-Smith notes its appeal as a Latin American alternative to Nordic systems. The country’s approach balances state responsibility with community and employer participation, though it remains a work in progress. Uruguay’s system reflects efforts to address demographic shifts, including a fertility rate of 1.2 and an aging population, while promoting gender equity by reducing unpaid care burdens on women.

item.title: Taiwan's Drone Industry Faces Challenges Amid Export Surge
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Taiwan’s drone industry looks like it's booming. Inside, the picture is much shakier.
Taiwan's drone exports surged 34 times from 2024 to 2025, reaching 191,373 units by June 2026, with most sales to Europe. However, industry insiders warn that weak supply chain management, poor coordination, and delayed military purchases threaten its ambitions. Export growth may reflect short-term demand from Ukraine's war effort rather than long-term stability. Taiwanese firms face challenges verifying China-free components, with one manufacturer, Jiin Ming, accused of using Chinese parts and submitting false certificates. Military procurement remains limited, with Taiwan's armed forces possessing fewer than 5,000 drones. A $7.6 billion funding plan for 210,000 drones by 2031 faces delays, risking industry growth. Testing is hindered by Taiwan's terrain, prompting some firms to test in Dubai. The government is establishing a drone committee and certification standards, but funding delays and unclear military requirements persist. Dennis Huang of Taiwan UAV noted the industry's competitiveness relies on the China-free supply chain. Cathy Fang of DSET warned that without sustained demand beyond wartime, Taiwan's position could be challenged by competitors developing their own alternatives.

item.title: Redwood Materials Repurposes Old EV Batteries for AI Energy Storage
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: The Tesla veteran helping turn old EV batteries into a new business powering AI
Colin Campbell, former Tesla engineer and Redwood Materials' CTO, is leading the company's expansion into energy storage using retired EV batteries to power AI data centers. Redwood, founded by Tesla co-founder JB Straubel, now repurposes old batteries for large-scale electricity storage, bypassing the need for new battery production. Campbell estimates this new business could surpass Redwood's original metals refining operations in scale. The company's Pack Manager device acts as a 'universal translator' enabling batteries from different automakers to work together. Redwood has partnered with AI firms like Crusoe and secured funding from Google and Nvidia. Campbell emphasizes the need for patient investors and innovative approaches to industrial challenges, noting that overlooked inefficiencies in energy systems present significant opportunities. He argues the business would thrive even without the current AI boom, as demand for reliable energy storage grows across industries.

item.title: Nick Bostrom claims AI could extend human lifespan to 1,400 years
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Living to 1,400 could be possible with AI. And that's a conservative estimate, Nick Bostrom says.
Nick Bostrom, a Swedish philosopher and former Oxford professor, claims AI could enable humans to live over 1,400 years by overcoming aging and reducing other mortality risks. Speaking on an A16z show episode, Bostrom said life expectancy without aging could reach 1,200 to 1,400 years, calling this a conservative lower bound. He emphasized that AI advancements in biomedicine and antiaging research could drastically extend lifespans. Bostrom, who founded the Future of Humanity Institute in 2005, noted the complexity of balancing rapid AI development with safety. He argued that delaying AI progress might save millions of lives but could increase existential risks. The institute closed in 2024. Bostrom acknowledged the trade-off between accelerating AI innovation and ensuring alignment with human interests, stating that more time spent on AI safety research could reduce risks but at the cost of delayed benefits.

item.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs due to financial losses
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter signed by CEO Jens Ritter and four board members. The decision follows an operating loss of €180 million in the first nine months of the year, averaging €20 million monthly. The board stated this is the third consecutive year of financial losses, with the letter noting Lufthansa is 'not competitive' in cost structure, efficiency, and productivity. Additional cost-saving measures include reducing employee travel benefits, restructuring hub operations, replacing A320 aircraft with A220 jets, and equipping ten aircraft monthly with Starlink for revenue. The time frame and connection to prior cuts remain unclear. Lufthansa also announced 4,000 administrative job cuts in September 2025 due to AI and digitalization. Rising fuel costs from the US-Israeli war with Iran further strain its financial outlook.

item.title: Poway Bans Drinking Water for Nonfunctional Turf Irrigation
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Poway moves to ban the use of drinking water for nonfunctional turf irrigation
Poway City Council approved an ordinance Nov. 17 to comply with Assembly Bill 1572, which bans using drinking water for nonfunctional turf irrigation on nonresidential properties. The rule targets ornamental turf not in recreational areas, excluding residential properties but including common areas managed by homeowners’ associations. Golf courses are exempt as commercial properties. Compliance phases begin Jan. 1, 2027, for state and municipal agencies, with other properties phased in by 2028. About 150-200 properties across 25 acres are affected. City officials estimate the ban could save 25 acre-feet of water annually. Mayor Steve Vaus called the state mandate an 'unfunded mandate,' while Utilities Administrator Carlos Cortes noted enforcement tools exist. The ordinance is set for adoption Dec. 1. More details are available through the California Water Efficiency Partnership.

item.title: Art Jury recommends approval of Silvergate development
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
Rancho Santa Fe Association Art Jury recommended board approval of Silvergate, a senior living development on a vacant lot near the community. The recommendation, made on Nov. 17, follows a two-year design review process with developer AmeriCare Health & Retirement. Association Building Commissioner Joel Levanetz stated the recommendation does not finalize project approval, which will be considered by the RSF Association Board of Directors in December. The next board meeting is scheduled for Dec. 3 at 10 a.m., though the agenda remains unset. Silvergate’s design includes age-restricted rental apartments, cottages, memory care units, and on-site amenities like a restaurant, spa, pool, and trails. The project will also undergo a separate county review requiring a major use permit, environmental impact studies, and public input.

item.title: Britons working past 67 rise 18% in four years
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Number of Britons working beyond age 67 up 18% in four years
The number of British people working beyond state pension age rose 18% in four years, reaching 860,000 individuals aged 67 or older. HMRC data shows payrolled workers aged 67-70 increased to 467,900, up 25% since 2022, while those working in their seventies rose 12% and eighties 15%. Financial planner Nicholas Clark attributed the trend to rising living costs and inadequate pension savings, noting many work out of necessity. Wealth manager analysis found the growth in older workers outpaced demographic growth by threefold. Age UK’s Chris Brooks called the trend largely positive for purpose and benefits but stressed the importance of retirement choice. Catherine Foot of Standard Life highlighted increased part-time work and career shifts, while noting middle earners tend to work longest. Clark urged people to assess savings against retirement needs, suggesting sacrifices now or maximizing pension allowances to avoid working into their seventies or eighties.

item.title: Transfer Credits Often Don't Count Toward Degrees, Report Shows
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Original headline: Transfer credits can be accepted and still not count toward a degree
A 2024 California State Auditor report found 21% of community college students who intended to transfer to four-year universities between 2017-2019 completed that goal within four years, with 15% of Hispanic or Latino students achieving it. Many transferred credits are accepted but do not apply to degree requirements, forcing students to retake courses. National University, which serves over 80% transfer students, uses transfer agreements to guarantee admission for those completing an Associate Degree for Transfer, preserving credits. However, credits from unrelated fields or incomplete degrees require individual review, leading to variable outcomes. The 2021 Joint Statement by three higher education associations outlined three criteria for credit evaluation: course quality, content alignment, and program relevance. The National Student Clearinghouse reported 71.2% of transfer students earned bachelor's degrees within six years. The State Auditor urged California's public universities to standardize transfer policies and expand the Associate Degree for Transfer. J.B. Robinson, National University's dean, noted students balance work, family, and education, emphasizing the need for clear credit pathways. Credit evaluations, provided before enrollment, determine which courses count toward degrees, often requiring repeated courses for students with limited time.

item.title: Small Businesses Stay Optimistic Amid Rising Costs and AI Adoption
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Why small businesses are staying optimistic, even as costs rise and AI takes hold
Rising costs are pushing small-business owners to raise prices, with 52% doing so in the past year and half planning to again next year. Gusto's survey of 1,731 owners shows cautious optimism despite economic uncertainty. Nich Tremper, Gusto's principal economist, noted owners feel more confident about their businesses than the broader economy, with 61% optimistic about their operations versus 18% for the U.S. economy. AI adoption is expanding beyond basic tasks, with 67% using it for customer data analysis and demand planning. Kyle Ray, founder of Geek Window Cleaning, uses AI tools to manage finances and customer service, calling them an 'AI CFO.' Cost pressures persist, with 59% citing rising material costs, but owners adapt by leveraging technology. Tremper emphasized small businesses face inflationary challenges but remain optimistic due to community reliance on their services.

item.title: Anthropic’s Wall Street stimulus fades
item.description:
Source: FT World
Anthropic's IPO drove Wall Street gains despite broader tech market declines. The company's stock surged 39% on its $83 listing price, closing at $97, benefiting founders, employees, and venture capitalists. However, retail investors received only 15% of their requested shares, with some calling the allocation process unfair. Investment banks Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley earned 41% of the $550mn fee pool, while JPMorgan and Citigroup took $55mn each. Despite the success, AI-related stocks have fallen this year as fears of market disruption persist. Revolut faces regulatory scrutiny over money laundering allegations in Italy, Sweden, and the UK. Meanwhile, Marvell's $115bn acquisition of Lumentum, aimed at expanding AI chip production, faces investor skepticism. Corporate moves include law firms reshuffling leadership and financial executives joining new roles. The article highlights the mixed outcomes of AI-driven deals and the challenges facing tech firms and financial institutions.

item.title: San Diego Gun Store Reports Rise in Firearm Sales, Attributes to Holiday Season
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: San Diego gun store sees firearm, ammo sales rise but says it’s not panic buying
San Diego gun store reports rise in firearm and ammunition sales, but owner Bryan Howes attributes the increase to the holiday season rather than panic buying. Howes notes the surge is 'more tempered' compared to pandemic-era spikes, when fear drove a surge in demand. He emphasizes the current trend is part of normal retail activity. Costco has seen generators sell out, with over 80% reported as unavailable. The San Diego Sheriff's Office states it is monitoring the situation but has no reports of law enforcement concerns. Howes advises against stockpiling, urging customers to 'relax, take a breath, and make a planned decision.'

item.title: Reddit User Asks for Financial Guidance After Job Loss
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Asked on Reddit: I Lost My Job; What Should I Do First?
A Redditor asked for advice after losing their job, seeking guidance on financial steps to take first. Financial experts recommended avoiding early retirement withdrawals, filing for unemployment, and reviewing severance packages carefully. Parker Wine, retirement planning advisor, urged patience to avoid impulsive decisions, emphasizing the need to weigh options before acting. John Rafferty, investment advisor, advised reviewing severance details, including health insurance options like COBRA, and creating a budget that prioritizes essentials like rent and utilities. He also suggested cutting non-essential spending and exploring low-cost activities to maintain mental well-being. Laura Adams, financial coach, highlighted the importance of connecting with friends and family to combat financial shame and emotional decision-making. Experts also stressed the value of emergency savings, ideally covering three to six months of expenses, and suggested starting side hustles like substitute teaching or ridesharing to supplement income. The Redditor noted many Americans lack emergency savings, adding urgency to the advice.

item.title: Anthropic shares trade on Nasdaq amid AI market speculation
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
Shares of Anthropic, a US AI company, began trading on Nasdaq on Thursday. The stock opened at $111.50, 34% above its $83 IPO price, valuing the company at $2 trillion. It closed at $97 per share. Anthropic raised $81 billion by offering 980 million shares, surpassing market estimates of $1.3 trillion. The company, known for its Claude chatbot, is the first major AI firm to go public. Competitor OpenAI has delayed its IPO to 2027. Anthropic carries $6.2 billion in debt and faces high costs for computing infrastructure, despite not yet turning a profit. Analysts warn that the AI sector's rapid growth may signal a potential bubble.

item.title: San Diego faces record high tides during Thanksgiving
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Largest high tides on record expected to hit San Diego coast over Thanksgiving holiday
San Diego County faces its tallest high tides on record during the Thanksgiving holiday, with tides reaching 8.20 feet next Wednesday and 8.10 feet on Thanksgiving Day. The National Weather Service attributes the extreme tides to El Niño, which warmed ocean temperatures to 73.6 degrees in La Jolla—12.1 degrees above average. Forecasters warn that strong swells from the south and northwest could push seawater inland, exacerbating flooding. A seawall collapse at Sunset Cliffs and seawater intrusion into streets and manholes have already occurred. The Port of San Diego has closed two trails until Nov. 30 to prevent erosion and instability. Samantha Zuber, a weather service forecaster, called the situation a potential problem due to combined tidal and swell impacts.

item.title: Army postpones lead azide detonation to Monday
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Original headline: Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday
The U.S. Army postponed a planned detonation of nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown until Monday, citing public safety concerns. Army Secretary Adam Telle announced the delay to avoid risks from a forecasted temperature drop, which could destabilize the material. Environmental groups Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed an emergency motion to halt the plan, arguing the EPA permit failed to address health and environmental risks or explore alternatives. The Army emphasized safety measures, including water saturation, sand barriers, and evacuations for nearby residents. Schools in the area, including those in Middletown, planned closures due to lead exposure concerns. The detonation, intended to safely dispose of degraded lead azide, faces criticism over communication and public notification. Senators Chuck Grassley, Josh Turek, and Rob Sand criticized the Army’s handling of the situation, calling for transparency. The Army stated destroying the material in place is the only responsible option due to its instability. Lead exposure risks, particularly for children, prompted additional precautions like indoor stays and surface cleaning after the event.

item.title: Erewhon's $749 Thanksgiving Feast Highlights L.A. Dining Divide
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Erewhon's $749 Thanksgiving feast and L.A.'s holiday dinner divide
Erewhon’s $749 Thanksgiving feast highlights L.A.’s dining divide. The average cost of a Thanksgiving meal for 10 people is $58.63, up 6.3% from 2025, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation. Retailers offer pre-made meals under $100, with Vallarta Supermarkets’ $89.99 feast serving eight and Ralphs’ $95 option. Erewhon’s organic meal, priced at $749, serves eight to 10 people at $74.90 per person. Food experts note the meal reflects a broader economic divide, as conventional stores aim for affordability while premium retailers cater to different demographics. Brandon Hau called the Erewhon feast a social experiment, while professors emphasized that such high-cost meals are not representative of U.S. affordability. Pre-made options cost more due to labor and convenience, though some consumers splurge on luxury meals. Whole Foods’ $599.99 meal includes multiple dishes and desserts, while Erewhon’s menu features free-range turkey, organic sides, and pumpkin pie. A commenter noted the meal’s serving size is unrealistic for most households.

item.title: Shoppers Buy Generators and Emergency Meals Amid Tech Failures
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Shoppers are stocking up on generators and emergency meals
Retailers report increased sales of emergency supplies as consumers stock up on generators, meal kits, and water amid tech failures and infrastructure concerns. Costco, Walmart, and Tractor Supply Co. saw spikes in preparedness items, with Costco's generators selling out rapidly. Mizuho analyst David Bellinger observed shoppers buying solar generators and pantry staples, noting 21 of 26 generators at Costco were sold out. Walmart confirmed higher sales of propane and water. Tractor Supply Co. VP Michael Cooper reported rising demand for fuel tanks, water barrels, and food preservation supplies, though the trend is broader than hurricane prep. Emergency meal kit sellers ReadyWise and My Patriot Supply faced order delays due to high demand, with shipping times extended to weeks. Experts recommend three days of water and non-perishable food, aligning with Red Cross guidelines. Anduril's Palmer Luckey advised three days of water and dry food. Heather Nianouris spent $1,200 on emergency supplies, including tarps, batteries, and canned goods, citing fears of being unprepared like during the pandemic.

item.title: Russian Missile Attack on Kyiv Damages Bridges, Kills at Least Eight
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle, FT World
Russian forces launched a major missile attack on Kyiv, striking three bridges and causing at least eight deaths. Over 100 missiles and 400 drones targeted infrastructure, including energy facilities, power lines, and bridges. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the assault 'one of the most massive strikes' of the war, accusing Russia of targeting civilians with 'double-tap strikes' and cluster munitions. Ukrainian officials confirmed 79 cruise missiles were intercepted, with fighter jets scrambled to counter the threat. The attack disrupted power in Kyiv and other regions, forcing nuclear plants to reduce output. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko closed three bridges and urged public transport use. Poland reported Russian missiles violated its airspace, with two landing near its border. Russia claimed strikes targeted energy infrastructure, transport hubs, and NATO-linked facilities. Zelensky demanded a 'clear response' from the global community. Ukraine’s military confirmed prior damage to the Crimean Bridge, which Moscow condemned as a 'far more painful' retaliation. The attack marked another escalation in the conflict, with strikes on critical infrastructure amid ongoing peace talks.
item.source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle, FT World

item.title: Chase, Mastercard, Visa warn of potential customer data exposure
item.description:
Source: Washington Post Original headline: Cyberattack may have exposed Chase Bank and Mastercard customer data
Cyberattackers may have accessed names and email addresses of some JPMorgan Chase and Mastercard customers through a third-party service provider, the companies said. Visa acknowledged awareness of data exposure claims but did not confirm breaches. None of the companies reported compromised payment data or system disruptions. The incident involved a third-party vendor, though none have named the provider or confirmed if breaches were linked. Mastercard stated a "limited amount of email addresses" were exposed, while Chase mentioned potential access to marketing data held by vendors. Both companies said the exposure was contained and affected customers would be contacted. Chase also noted a separate service disruption earlier this week caused by a software bug, which is unrelated to the current incident. Recent global tech outages and disruptions have heightened customer concerns about cyberthreats.

item.title: Xi Commends Australia-China Relations Turnaround
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: China's Xi praises 'turnaround' in relationship with Australia
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chinese President Xi Jinping met at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, with Xi calling the relationship a 'comprehensive turnaround' since Albanese took office in 2022. Xi highlighted cooperation in agriculture, energy, green economy, and AI, while Albanese emphasized constructive engagement with China. China remains Australia's top trading partner, though tensions peaked under the previous government's coronavirus inquiry, leading to $13 billion in import curbs. Since Albanese's Labor government, most restrictions have been lifted, but disputes over missile tests and foreign investment screens persist. Albanese reiterated the need to manage differences, noting China's actions impact Australia. He will meet Premier Li Qiang later, with a business roundtable involving Australian mining firms and Chinese executives addressing iron ore trade concerns. Australia criticized China's central buying body for iron ore as increasing bargaining power.

item.title: San Diego Pilot Identified as Ocotillo Wells Plane Crash Victim
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Pilot killed in Ocotillo Wells plane crash identified as San Diego man
A 64-year-old private pilot from San Diego, Ray Ellis, died when the light plane he was flying crashed into a desert hillside in Ocotillo Wells on November 3. The Piper PA-22 went down shortly before 9:30 a.m. off Quarry Road, near state Route 78. Authorities identified Ellis as the sole occupant of the aircraft. A sheriff’s helicopter crew located the burned wreckage on Blowsand Hill in the Ocotillo Wells State Vehicular Recreation Area. Cal Fire crews later recovered his body from the crash site. The Federal Aviation Administration and county officials are investigating the cause of the accident. No other individuals were involved in the incident.

item.title: Woman buys Ford Bronco to drive home during FAA ground stop
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Woman buys Ford Bronco and drives 27 hours to get home during FAA ground stop
Tara Harding, 40, bought a Ford Bronco for $48,000 on Nov. 13 to drive 27 hours home to North Dakota after FAA ground stop halted flights. The FAA ordered a national ground stop due to a router issue disrupting air-traffic control, canceling thousands of flights. Harding, owner of Simply You Wellness Clinic, and two employees were stranded at Charlotte airport after their evening flight was canceled. With no rental cars or alternative transport available, she opted for a Ford Bronco after her husband suggested it. She financed the vehicle with $0 down, securing it by 9:06 p.m. despite dealership closing at 8 p.m. The trio drove 1,593 miles, trading driving shifts. Harding plans to keep the Bronco, naming it Charlotte, and may join a Bronco club. Ford praised her choice, calling it a testament to the brand.

item.title: Worker dies after electrical injury in San Diego MTS substation
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
Patrick Pryor, 42, a San Diego Metropolitan Transit System maintenance worker, died after an electrical injury at a substation near trolley tracks in Stockton on Nov. 13. The Medical Examiner’s Office confirmed he was taken to a hospital and died about half an hour before midnight. Pryor, who had worked for MTS since 2006 and held the rank of journeyman Wayside Electromechanic since 2011, was described by CEO Sharon Cooney as a mentor who trained many apprentices. Cooney called the incident a 'heartbreaking loss' for the agency and noted MTS is collaborating with the state’s Division of Occupational Safety and Health. Union representative Peter Kennedy described the news as 'devastating' after receiving the call on Friday morning.

item.title: Pakistani Minister Visits Delhi for SCO Forum Amid Strained Relations
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: India: Pakistani minister visits Delhi for SCO forum amid frozen ties
Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik arrived in New Delhi for a Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) cultural forum, marking the first ministerial visit to India since 2023. The visit follows a four-day India-Pakistan conflict in 2025 and comes amid frozen bilateral relations. Opposition leaders criticized the government for hosting Malik, with Samajwadi Party leader Fakhrul Hasan Chand accusing the BJP of hypocrisy. Meanwhile, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) accused India of targeting Muslims during a voter roll revision that removed 130 million names, calling it a 'country of particular concern.' India's Election Commission defended the process as removing duplicates and ineligible voters. Cyclone Akvan made landfall on India's eastern coast, causing no major damage. Rahul Gandhi criticized India's global role, prompting BJP backlash. The SCO forum, led by PM Narendra Modi, aims to foster civilizational dialogue, though no breakthrough in relations is expected.

item.title: NIH Releases Last Lab-Chimpanzees to Sanctuary in Louisiana
item.description:
Source: Washington Post Original headline: The NIH is releasing the last chimpanzees used for lab testing
The NIH is releasing its final group of research chimpanzees to Chimp Haven, a federal sanctuary in Keithville, Louisiana. The 33 primates will relocate next year from the Keeling Center in Texas to the sanctuary, which houses over 250 chimps. Rana Smith, Chimp Haven's CEO, emphasized that the chimps will engage in natural behaviors like climbing, foraging, and socializing. The sanctuary previously received 21 chimps from the Alamogordo Primate Facility in 2025, a decade after the government banned invasive testing on chimpanzees. Kathleen Conlee of Humane World for Animals noted the primates were used in past biomedical research, including AIDS studies. The NIH has not disclosed the chimps' identities but plans activities like violin concerts, food puzzles, and film screenings. Smith mentioned some chimps enjoy watching movies, including Bollywood and musicals.

item.title: Oil Prices Lose Bond Market Link as Inflation Pressures Persist
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Oil loses grip on bond markets as inflation ‘virus’ spreads
The strong link between oil prices and bond yields has weakened as central banks prioritize inflation control over energy markets. Despite falling crude prices, U.S. 10-year Treasury yields remain above 5%, reflecting persistent inflation concerns. Vanguard’s Ales Koutny noted bonds have 'untethered from oil' and returned to their usual behavior. The correlation between oil and bonds peaked at 65% in September but dropped to under 20% as traders shifted focus to central bank policies. Fed rate hikes, including a September increase and expected December action, have kept yields elevated. UK inflation pressures also drive Bank of England rate expectations, with a 75% chance of another hike. Investors warn inflationary trends are entrenched, with Greg Peters calling it an 'inflation virus' hard to eliminate. As oil’s influence wanes, bonds are regaining their role as safe havens amid stock market volatility.

item.title: UK and EU to Launch Youth Mobility Scheme for 100,000 Young People
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
The UK and EU plan to launch a youth mobility scheme allowing up to 100,000 young people from each region to work and study in the other’s country. The agreement, expected at the UK-EU summit in Brussels, faces challenges over UK demands to limit numbers and EU insistence that EU students pay the same tuition fees as domestic students. Prime Minister’s Office officials noted ongoing talks on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing. Labour leader Andy Burnham emphasized potential benefits like lower food prices and reduced bureaucracy, while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch criticized the deal as reopening Brexit divisions. The UK’s request to cap migrant numbers remains a key negotiation hurdle. Burnham also pushed for a Channel action plan on immigration cooperation. Meanwhile, Reform UK’s Nigel Farage condemned the deal as a costly error, questioning Labour’s democratic mandate. Labour’s 2024 manifesto explicitly rejects rejoining the EU or the single market. Former deputy PM David Lammy urged the PM to promise EU reentry, but cabinet divisions persist over Brexit reversal costs.

item.title: Storm Brings Rain, Winds, High Surf to Mission Beach
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Rain, strong winds and high surf hit Mission Beach as latest storm moves through San Diego
Rain, strong winds, and high surf hit Mission Beach as a storm moved through San Diego. Sand and seaweed covered the boardwalk, with businesses moving merchandise indoors. Crews used tractors to reinforce beach berms. Residents and visitors noted the storm's intensity, with San Diego resident Wesley Currie calling it more severe than usual. Maria Rey, visiting from Texas, described conditions as unlike anything she'd seen in decades. Beachgoers were warned about rip currents and large waves. Dan Jackson ran despite the weather, saying San Diegans make the most of stormy days. Currie noted higher tides and larger waves compared to past storms. A beach hazards statement remains in effect through Friday, with king tides expected next week along the San Diego County coastline.

item.title: China Warns Against Off-Season Mount Fuji Climbing Amid Reward Offer
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
The Chinese embassy in Japan warned citizens against off-season Mount Fuji climbs after a missing hiker's family offered a reward. Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November while climbing during the closed season. His family is offering 500,000 yuan for his safe return and 100,000 yuan for his body. Embassy officials cited risks like strong winds and blizzards, noting shelters and first-aid centers are closed during off-season. Mount Fuji's official climbing season is July to September. Yamanashi province announced new rules requiring off-season climbers to submit detailed plans and pay for helicopter rescues. Governor Kotaro Nagasaki warned that search efforts for Chen could cause 'secondary disasters' and urged the family to avoid actions endangering others. Chen's friends turned back after realizing the mountain was closed, but he continued alone. A friend last saw him at 10:30 on 8 November. Local authorities suspended searches due to weather. Chen's father arrived in Japan on 13 November, but the reward's posting date is unclear.

item.title: Iran's 'Boiling Frog' Strategy Faces Uncertain Future
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Original headline: Iran’s ‘Boiling Frog’ Strategy
Iran's strategy to gradually increase pressure on the U.S. and Western nations through economic disruptions is seen as a 'boiling frog' approach, according to Vali Nasr. He argues that sustained disruptions to the global economy serve as leverage to influence Western leaders' actions. Nasr notes that Iran views the U.S. midterm election results as proof of this strategy's effectiveness, though the long-term viability of the current blockade remains uncertain. The U.S. faces challenges maintaining the blockade due to financial and logistical constraints, while Iran continues to escalate attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Trump's options are limited: he cannot escalate militarily without risking retaliation, nor can he abandon the blockade without appearing weak. Nasr suggests the new Democratic-controlled Congress may push for diplomacy, but Trump's unpredictability and focus on his legacy complicate efforts. Iran's goal is to deter Western action by threatening regional and global economic chaos, though the strategy's sustainability is in question. Nasr warns that the current approach may collapse under its own weight or lead to renewed conflict if tensions escalate further.

item.title: International Court Rules Myanmar Guilty of Genocide Against Rohingya
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News, BBC News, Washington Post - World Original headline: International Court of Justice Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
The International Court of Justice ruled Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, marking the first state conviction under the 1948 Genocide Convention. Judges voted 9-6, citing evidence of 10,000 Rohingya deaths, 392 villages burned, and systematic sexual violence. Myanmar's government denied allegations, claiming operations were counterinsurgency, but the court rejected this, stating the violence exceeded counterterrorism scope. Judge Yuji Iwasawa noted the methods 'are not consistent with counterinsurgency operations.' The ruling also found Myanmar violated the convention through discriminatory policies eroding Rohingya rights. Myanmar must provide reparations, including safe return for nearly a million refugees, prosecute perpetrators, and pay compensation. ICJ rulings are binding but require UN Security Council enforcement. Rohingya survivors and leaders expressed hope, with one calling the decision 'emotional and historic.' Legal experts highlighted potential influence on future cases, including South Africa's case against Israel. The case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, acknowledged Arsa's attacks but found Myanmar's hate speech and policies made mass violence likely. The ruling underscores global implications, urging international action on Myanmar's actions and Rohingya rights.
item.source: NPR Topics: News, BBC News, Washington Post - World

item.title: Creators Turn Film Cameras into Viral Business with 8M Followers
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: These creators built a 7-figure business by giving film cameras to strangers
Grant Weintrob and cofounders Christian Baiocco and Griffin Katz built a seven-figure business by giving strangers disposable film cameras to capture candid moments, which they edit into viral videos. Launched in 2023, the project 'Life on Film' gained traction by blending man-on-the-street storytelling with nostalgic analog aesthetics, amassing 8 million followers and 2 billion views. Brands like Nike, Microsoft, and Fujifilm partner with the team, which uses analog cameras to counter AI-driven distrust and tap into Gen Z's analog revival. Revenue comes from brand deals and ad revenue, with plans to expand into direct-to-consumer products. The team emphasizes unscripted, authentic content, avoiding staged setups except for branded videos. Despite risks like equipment failure and theft, they continue approaching strangers in public spaces, aiming to create cinematic short films and eventually a studio for unscripted series. Their success has drawn attention from Hollywood and streamers, positioning them as a hybrid between A24 and Humans of New York.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Rise to 7.38% on November 19
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Mortgage Rates Today, Thursday, November 19: Kind of a Big Jump
Mortgage rates surged to 7.38% APR on November 19, up 25 basis points from the prior day and 12 basis points from a week earlier. The increase follows mixed inflation data, including a 0.3% monthly rise in producer prices and a 6.5% year-over-year increase, signaling potential future cost hikes. Investors expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again in December, which typically drives up mortgage rates. Homeowners are advised to consider refinancing if current rates are at least 0.5-0.75 percentage points lower than their existing rate, though few qualify given current levels. Lenders adjust rates daily based on market conditions, making rate locks advisable for those with favorable quotes. Personalized rate quotes vary due to factors like credit scores and down payments, and applicants should focus on affordability rather than chasing lower rates. Preapproval and comparing lender offers are recommended steps for those planning to buy or refinance.
